data.reason: The KPI's main goal is town-wide on_time_deliveries, with the customer-wait metrics p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished as watched goals (decision K1). Option 1 is the only option that moves the main goal substantially: on-time rises from 121.8 to 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds) and late falls from 10.4 to 1.2. It also improves every customer-facing metric that does not depend on the promise. p95_wait_s falls from 188 to 81.4 and max_wait_s from 385 to 245, unfinished stays at 0.0, and the lowest on-time rate rises from 0.84 to 0.98. Option 1 passed check, the constitution and the KPI conditions. Option 3 gives only +0.8 on 3/5 seeds and leaves customer waits unchanged (p95_wait_s 188, max_wait_s 385). It weakens the promise to customers, who do not vote, and gives them no faster service, so its unanimous vote does not justify a change that is worse for customers. Keep leaves about 10 late deliveries and long waits in place. I am choosing against the B and C votes. The vote is an input, but the KPI the operator set is about customers across the town, and customers have no vote. B's loss is small (38.9 to 37.2). C's loss is large (28.8 to 19.0), and I acknowledge it as a real cost that needs a negotiated mitigation rather than being ignored. The rise in road violations from 25.8 to 34.0 is the main risk. It passed the constitution, but its cause has not been examined. I am therefore adopting option 1 as a rule-level change that can be reverted, with explicit follow-ups. If the violations prove safety-relevant, or C cannot be mitigated, I will revert to block_k 3 or measure intermediate settings. I take responsibility for this override on behalf of the operator.
assumptions: The constitution allows a human (or an LLM acting for the operator) to adopt a rule change that passed check and the constitution despite a majority 'no' vote.
The road violations added under option 1 are not safety-critical, given that it passed the constitution's invariants.
The 5-seed measurements represent next period's demand well enough.
Companies will not change their behaviour enough under block_k 2 to erase the gain in the next period.
block_k can be reverted to 3 at the next period if problems appear.
unknowns: The cause and severity of the rise in road violations from 25.8 to 34.0.
Why C loses so much utility, and which mitigation (eviction order, compensation) C would accept.
Whether B and C will respond strategically, for example by changing their votes on future proposals or their routing behaviour.
Whether intermediate settings or combinations, such as option 1 plus other rule tweaks, would keep most of the gain at less cost to C.
Robustness under different demand levels, beyond the 5 measured seeds.

predictions.subject: metric:road_violations
predictions.note: Measured 25.8 -> 34.0; this is the main cost to monitor.

follow_ups.text: Break down the road violations added under block_k 2 by type and check whether any are safety-relevant. If any are, revert to block_k 3 or propose a guard.
Analyse why C's robots are evicted more often, and propose a mitigation (eviction order, hold rules or compensation) that C and B could vote for. Measure it on the same seeds.
Measure intermediate or alternative settings, such as block_k 2 with a fairness-aware eviction order, to see whether they keep the on-time gain at less cost to C.
Re-check on_time_deliveries, p95_wait_s and max_wait_s under next period's real demand, and confirm the gain holds outside the 5 measured seeds.
